The Settlement and the Dictators

Depression and Dictators: Stalin, Mussolini, Hitler

Mini-lesson · Mr. Magister

Democracy Gives Way

11923: Weimar Germany and hyperinflation
21929: the Depression
3Stalin: Five-Year Plans and the Purge
4Mussolini: the March on Rome

Today's Focus

How did a Europe full of democracies in 1920 become a Europe of dictators, and how much was conditions and how much was choices?

In 1920 Europe had more democracies than it ever had before. By 1939 many of them had given way to dictators. Today you will meet three of those men, see how they gained power, and ask how far their rise was a matter of conditions and how far a matter of choices.

Objectives
  1. Describe how the Great Depression weakened democracies and helped dictators rise.
  2. Compare how Stalin, Mussolini, and Hitler came to power and how each ruled.
  3. Evaluate how much each rise depended on the choices of particular people and how much on larger conditions.
Quick Check-in

In 1920 Europe had more democracies than ever. Before you read: what do you think did the most to bring dictators to power?

The Book

Parts 1 to 6

⚡ DECIDE FIRST
It is 1932. Banks are failing, trade is shrinking, and about one worker in four has no job. You lead a democratic government.
Decide first, and jot your answer in your notebook: what could you try, and what could go wrong with each choice? Then open to compare.
Britain and the United States kept their constitutions and tried new policies. In Germany the republic already stood on borrowed money, and the collapse in the value of money in 1923 had wiped out the savings of the middle class. Hard times did not push every country the same way. Frightened people did listen to those who promised strong action, but what happened next still depended on choices made by particular leaders, which is the question this lesson keeps asking.
⚡ HOW MUCH?
Millions of Soviet peasants starved in the early 1930s. How much of that famine came from decisions made by the state?
⚡ PUT IT IN ORDER
Tap these events in the order they happened, earliest first.

    Part 1

    Weimar Germany

    Chapter 1Weimar Germany
    Chapter 1

    Weimar Germany

    After the Kaiser fell, Germany became a republic with a constitution written in the city of Weimar. It had a parliament, a president, and wide freedoms. But many Germans saw it as the government that had signed the hated treaty. In 1923 Germany fell behind on reparations, and French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, the coal and steel heartland. The government printed money to pay striking workers, and hyperinflation followed. A loaf of bread cost billions of marks. The savings of the middle class vanished.

    It helps to see how money died. By late 1923 prices were doubling in days, and the German mark stood at several trillion to the American dollar. Workers were paid twice a day, and wives waited at the factory gate to rush the notes to the shops before they lost their value. Families whose savings, pensions, and insurance had been counted in marks found them worth less than a loaf of bread. Those who owed money could pay off a debt with a handful of notes. Many middle-class Germans blamed the republic, not the war or the printing presses, and the ruin stayed in the memory of a whole generation. A new currency introduced in November 1923 ended the crisis.

    Recovery followed. American loans under the Dawes Plan of 1924 eased the burden, and the foreign minister Gustav Stresemann made peace with France at Locarno in 1925. For a few years Germany seemed to be stable. But the republic stood on borrowed money and borrowed time.

    The republic also had a hidden weakness in its constitution. Its president had the power to issue emergency decrees under a clause called Article 48, which meant that a government unable to win a majority in parliament could still rule, as long as the president agreed. And with many small parties, no government held a firm majority for long. Stresemann, the one leader trusted abroad and at home, died in October 1929, only weeks before the American crash.

    Part 2

    The Great Depression

    Chapter 2The Great Depression
    Chapter 2

    The Great Depression

    In October 1929 the American stock market crashed. Banks failed, and American lenders called in their loans from abroad. World trade shrank as nations raised tariffs to protect their own industries. By 1932 about one American worker in four had no job. In Germany roughly six million were out of work. Governments in every democracy struggled to respond. Britain and the United States kept their constitutions and tried new policies. In Germany and several other countries, frightened citizens began to listen to people who promised strong action.

    Germany was hit harder than most because its recovery had been paid for with American loans. When those were called in, German banks failed, factories closed, and by 1932 about one worker in three had no job. The chancellor, Heinrich Brüning, a decent and cautious man, answered by cutting government spending and ruling by decree, which deepened the misery. Voters turned from the middle parties toward the extremes, the Communists and the Nazis. In Britain, a coalition took charge in 1931, and in the United States, President Franklin Roosevelt took office in March 1933 and began a flood of new programs known as the New Deal. Both democracies bent, and neither broke.

    Part 3

    Stalin: A Revolution from Above

    Chapter 3Stalin: A Revolution from Above
    Chapter 3

    Stalin: A Revolution from Above

    In the Soviet Union, Lenin's successor was Joseph Stalin, a cautious-looking man who held the dull-sounding post of General Secretary of the party. He used it to build a following, and by 1928 he had outmaneuvered the more brilliant Leon Trotsky, who was later exiled and, in 1940, murdered in Mexico on Stalin's order. Stalin then launched a Five-Year Plan to turn the Soviet Union into an industrial power at breakneck speed. New steel towns such as Magnitogorsk rose out of the plains, and heavy industry grew very fast.

    Stalin's rise rested on timing and patience. Lenin, ill in his last months, dictated notes warning that Stalin was too rude and had gathered too much power, and he suggested removing him as General Secretary. The party leaders chose not to publish the notes. Stalin then joined first with some rivals against Trotsky, and then with others against his former allies, defeating each in turn. The Five-Year Plan set targets from above, and when factories fell short the targets were raised again. Magnitogorsk was built beside an iron mountain by workers living in tents and barracks, with the help of American engineers, and it was meant to rival the steel towns of the Ruhr and Pittsburgh.

    The price was paid by the peasants. Under collectivization, the state seized their farms and herds and combined them into large collective farms. The wealthier peasants, called kulaks, were labeled enemies, and many were shot or deported to camps. Peasants killed their animals instead of surrendering them. Between 1932 and 1933 a terrible famine struck Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and southern Russia, and millions starved while the state continued to take grain. Historians estimate that five to seven million died in the whole Soviet Union. Then, in the Great Purge of 1936 to 1938, Stalin turned on the party itself. Show trials forced old Bolsheviks to confess to imaginary crimes, and hundreds of thousands were shot. Millions more went to the labor camps of the Gulag. This system, in which a single party and leader tried to control almost every part of life, is called totalitarianism.

    The Ukrainian famine shows how the system worked. Quotas for grain were set so high that peasants had nothing left, and the villages that fell short were punished by having food and goods taken away. In January 1933 the government closed the borders of Ukraine and the nearby Kuban region to travelers, so that starving peasants could not leave in search of bread. The Great Purge began after the murder of a popular party leader, Sergei Kirov, in December 1934. At the show trials, old comrades of Lenin confessed and were shot. In 1937 the purge reached the Red Army, and most of its top officers were removed or killed. Within a few years Stalin had cleared the party of nearly every man who remembered a Russia without him.

    Part 4

    Mussolini: The First Fascist

    Chapter 4Mussolini: The First Fascist
    Chapter 4

    Mussolini: The First Fascist

    Italy was on the winning side but felt cheated, and many Italians spoke of a mutilated victory. Prices rose, strikes spread, and the government seemed helpless. Benito Mussolini, a former socialist journalist, formed a movement in 1919 that took its name from the fasces, the bundle of rods and an axe carried by Roman officials. His Blackshirts beat up socialists and broke strikes. This movement is known as fascism. It praised the nation above the individual, rejected democracy, and glorified action and war.

    In October 1922 the Fascists announced a March on Rome. The army could have stopped them, but King Victor Emmanuel III chose not to call it out, and he asked Mussolini to form a government. A different decision by one man might have ended Fascism that week. By 1926 Mussolini had banned other parties and taken the title Duce. He made peace with the Church in the Lateran Treaty of 1929, which created Vatican City. In 1935 he invaded Ethiopia, and the League of Nations failed to stop him.

    The March on Rome was less of a march than a bluff. The Blackshirts who gathered numbered perhaps twenty-five thousand, poorly armed and soaked by rain, and a few regular soldiers could have scattered them. The prime minister prepared a decree of martial law, but the king refused to sign it. Mussolini, waiting in Milan, took a sleeping car to Rome only after the king invited him. He was thirty-nine, the youngest prime minister Italy had had. At first he ruled with other parties. In 1924 the Fascists killed Giacomo Matteotti, a Socialist deputy who had denounced their violence, and in January 1925 Mussolini told parliament that he took responsibility. Over the next two years he made himself dictator. In Ethiopia his army used poison gas. The League voted sanctions, but it left oil off the list, and Mussolini went on.

    Part 5

    Hitler: The Road to Power

    Chapter 5Hitler: The Road to Power
    Chapter 5

    Hitler: The Road to Power

    Adolf Hitler was born in Austria in 1889. He served as a corporal in the German army, and the defeat of 1918 left him bitter. He joined a small party that became the Nazi Party, and its violent hatred of Jews, communists, and the Versailles treaty became its message. After his failed attempt to seize power in Munich in 1923, he spent months in prison, where he wrote Mein Kampf. He decided to win power by elections.

    Hitler's early life had been a string of failures. He wanted to be an artist, but he was twice rejected by the art academy in Vienna, and he drifted through poor lodging houses before the war. In the army he was decorated for bravery. The Munich attempt, in November 1923, came at the height of the inflation. Hitler and his followers burst into a beer hall and then marched into the streets, where police fired and sixteen Nazis were killed. Hitler was convicted of treason, but the judges were friendly, and he served less than a year.

    For years it did not work. In 1928 the Nazis won under three percent of the vote. Then the Depression hit. By July 1932 the party won thirty-seven percent, more than any other, though never a majority. A group of conservatives, including the former chancellor Franz von Papen, thought they could use Hitler and control him. They persuaded President Hindenburg, and on January 30, 1933, Hitler was named chancellor. This was legal, and it was not inevitable. A different decision by a few old men in Berlin might have kept him out.

    The mechanism of those last months is worth following. After the election of September 1930, when the Nazis jumped to over eighteen percent, the chancellors depended on the president's decrees, and Hindenburg ruled with a small circle of advisers. In the next election, in November 1932, the Nazi vote fell to thirty-three percent, and the party was running short of money. Papen, who had been chancellor himself that year, saw a chance to return to power through Hitler. Hindenburg disliked the former corporal, but he gave way. Only two other Nazis sat in the new cabinet of eleven. Papen's circle believed they had hired a man they could manage.

    Hitler moved fast. After a fire destroyed the Reichstag building in February, he persuaded the president to suspend civil liberties. In March the parliament passed the Enabling Act, giving him power to make laws alone. Other parties were banned, unions dissolved, and the press brought under control. The first concentration camp opened at Dachau. When Hindenburg died in August 1934, Hitler took his powers and the title Führer. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935, which you will read, took citizenship from German Jews and began the legal persecution that led to catastrophe.

    The Enabling Act came on a vote that was not free. Armed Nazi storm troopers stood in and around the hall, and the Communist deputies had already been arrested or driven away. The act passed by 444 to 94, with only the Social Democrats voting no. In April 1933 a law removed Jews from the civil service, and soon Jewish doctors, lawyers, and professors were pushed from their jobs. In June 1934, in the Night of the Long Knives, Hitler had the leaders of his own storm troopers murdered, along with several old enemies. The army was relieved, and after Hindenburg's death its officers swore an oath to Hitler by name.

    Part 6

    Why Did Free Peoples Choose Them?

    Chapter 6Why Did Free Peoples Choose Them?
    Chapter 6

    Why Did Free Peoples Choose Them?

    The three men ruled differently, but they shared much: one party, one leader, a secret police, control of the press and schools, and the identification of an enemy within. They took advantage of fear, humiliation, and economic ruin. But in each case the outcome rested on particular decisions, by kings, presidents, and generals who could have acted otherwise. In this week's discussion you will weigh a question that follows: was the Treaty of Versailles too harsh or too weak, and how much does it explain? Think about all the causes you have met, and decide which ones mattered most.
